data.title: Debugger Detection and Evasion
data.summary: The sample checks for an attached debugger and alters its behaviour — refusing to run, running down a decoy path, or crashing the debugger — rather than execute normally under observation.
data.description:
Checks of this kind are cheap for the author and expensive for the analyst: a call to
IsDebuggerPresent, a read of the PEB's BeingDebugged flag, a timing check around a
single-stepped instruction, or an INT 2D / INT 3 probe that behaves differently once a
debugger has claimed the exception. None of these require the malware to know which
debugger is attached, only that one is.

Where the check succeeds, the sample most commonly takes a silent exit or branches into
decoy logic that looks plausible to a cursory read but does nothing. Confirming this
behaviour as debugger evasion, rather than an unrelated crash, usually needs a second run
with the check patched out or bypassed at the API level.
data.recommendation:
* Patch or hook the specific check (PEB flag, API return value, exception behaviour) rather than fighting the debugger generically.
* Re-run analysis with the check neutralised and diff the two execution paths — the branch not taken under observation is usually the interesting one.
* Record the exact check used; it is often reused unchanged across a family's samples and is a fast identification signal.
data.short_recommendation: Identify and neutralise the specific debugger check rather than the debugger's presence generically.

mitre_techniques.procedure: Behaviour differed under an attached debugger; confirmed by patching the check and re-running.
